facts.statement: Panoplosaurus lived in Alberta, Canada, during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus is a genus of armoured dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: All known specimens of Panoplosaurus come from the middle Campanian age of the Dinosaur Park Formation, dating to roughly 76 to 75 million years ago.
facts.quote: Few specimens of the genus are known, all from the middle Campanian of the Dinosaur Park Formation, roughly 76 to 75 million years ago.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was discovered in 1917 and named in 1919 by Lawrence Lambe, who derived the name from the Greek word for "well-armoured lizard".
facts.quote: It was first discovered in 1917, and named in 1919 by Lawrence Lambe, named for its extensive armour, meaning "well-armoured lizard".

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was a quadrupedal dinosaur approximately 5 meters long and weighing 1600 kilograms.
facts.quote: It was a quadrupedal animal, roughly 5 m long and 1600 kg in weight.

facts.statement: The skull of Panoplosaurus featured a short, domed snout and bony plates covering the cheeks.
facts.quote: The skull has a short snout, with a very domed surface, and bony plates directly covering the cheek.

facts.statement: Modern phylogenetic analyses place Panoplosaurus in the clade Panoplosaurini, close to Edmontonia and Animantarx, but distinct from Nodosaurus and Struthiosaurus.
facts.quote: Following consistent placements in phylogenetic analyses close to Edmontonia and the American taxon Animantarx, Panoplosaurus was placed into the clade Panoplosaurini, related but not close to Nodosaurus or Struthiosaurus, which it was considered close to around when it was named.

facts.statement: In 1917, Charles M. Sternberg discovered a nearly complete skull and skeleton of Panoplosaurus in Quarry 69 of the Belly River Group, 210 feet above sea level.
facts.quote: In 1917, Canadian paleontologist Charles M. Sternberg of the Geological Survey of Canada discovered a complete skull and significant amount of the skeleton of an armoured dinosaur in the sandstone layers of Quarry 69 of the Belly River Group, 210 ft above sea level.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen CMN 2759 includes a nearly complete skull, most cervical and front dorsal vertebrae with armor, a majority of the forelimb with three articulated fingers, pelvic fragments, foot bones, and hundreds of osteoderms.
facts.quote: The specimen, designated by the Canadian Museum of Nature accession number CMN 2759, and excavated 2.75 mi south of the mouth of the Little Sandhill tributary of the Red Deer River in Alberta, includes a nearly complete skull in articulation, most or all of the cervical vertebrae and the front dorsal vertebrae, and armour plates covering them, a majority of the disarticulated forelimb and three articulated fingers, a fragment of the pelvis and partial sacrum, a few bones of the foot, and multiple hundreds of osteoderms and dermal ossicles.

facts.statement: The geological formation containing the holotype was originally called the Belly River beds but is now classified as the upper level of the Dinosaur Park Formation from the late middle Campanian.
facts.quote: While the beds of discovery of the holotype, CMN 2759, were originally described as the Belly River beds, they are now considered part of the upper level of the Dinosaur Park Formation, pertaining to the late middle Campanian, 75 to 76 million years ago.

facts.statement: A scapula from New Mexico was referred to Panoplosaurus in 1981, but it may actually belong to Nodocephalosaurus due to age and location differences, though this remains uncertain.
facts.quote: A scapula from the Naashoibito member of the Kirtland Formation in New Mexico was referred to Panoplosaurus in 1981, but as it is from a different age and location from other specimens, may instead represent the ankylosaurid taxon Nodocephalosaurus, although this is uncertain due to lack of overlapping material.

facts.statement: In 2016, researchers Arbour and Currie restricted the genus Panoplosaurus to only the holotype specimen due to uncertainties regarding other referred specimens.
facts.quote: Arbour and Philip J. Currie further restricted Panoplosaurus to just the holotype in 2016, as a result of uncertainties surrounding the referrals of various specimens between it, Edmontonia rugosidens and Edmontonia longiceps, all from the Dinosaur Park Formation and similar deposits.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus weighed 1600 kg, making it comparable in size to other ankylosaurs from the region and heavier than or equal to its contemporary predators.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus was a rather large animal at 1600 kg, a comparable size to other ankylosaurs from the same location, and heavier than or approximately equivalent to all predators it coexisted with.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was about 5 meters long and lacked prominent spikes on its body, unlike many other ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus was about 5 m long, and was armoured like most ankylosaurs, but lacked prominent spikes anywhere on its body.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Panoplosaurus features a prominent armor plate covering the cheek, which may be a unique trait of the species or just an individual characteristic.
facts.quote: There is also a prominent armour plate covering the cheek in the type specimen of Panoplosaurus, which may be unique feature of the taxon, or individual, depending on what additional skulls are referred to P. mirus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Panoplosaurus and Edmontonia are the same taxon, which has complicated interpretations of their distribution and phylogeny.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus has at times been considered the proper name for material otherwise referred to as Edmontonia, complicating its phylogenetic and ecological interpretations, at one point being considered to have existed across Alberta, New Mexico and Texas, with specimens in institutions from Canada and the United States.

facts.statement: Researchers disagree on whether certain specimens, such as ROM 1215, belong to Panoplosaurus or Edmontonia, with some studies retaining them in Panoplosaurus and others moving them to Edmontonia.
facts.quote: The referral of ROM 1215 to Panoplosaurus was questioned by Coombs in 1990, and Roland A. Gangloff referred it and the Alaskan specimen DPMWA 90–25 to Edmontonia in 1995 based on the anatomy of the lack of diagnostic traits, but Victoria Arbour and colleagues retained ROM 1215 in Panoplosaurus in 2009, limiting the genus to it, the holotype CMN 2759, and specimen AMNH 3072, all from the upper Dinosaur Park Formation.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus had a broad, depressed skull that narrowed to a blunt, triangular snout.
facts.quote: The skull of Panoplosaurus is broad and depressed, narrowing towards the end of the blunt snout to form a triangular shape.

facts.statement: The skull of Panoplosaurus measured 335 mm in straight-line length but 530 mm across the curved roof.
facts.quote: At a total length of 335 mm in a straight line, the skull is curved in a way that across the skull roof the same length is 530 mm.

facts.statement: The skull of Panoplosaurus reached a maximum width of 295 mm behind the eye sockets, creating a short and broad profile.
facts.quote: Behind the orbits, the skull reaches its maximum width of 295 mm, giving it a very short and broad appearance.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus possessed very small eye sockets set far back from a squared snout with laterally open nostrils.
facts.quote: The orbits of Panoplosaurus are very small, and placed far from the snout, which is very squared and bearing laterally open nostrils.

facts.statement: The entire exterior of the Panoplosaurus skull was covered in bony plates, including large osteoderms on the sides and mandible, small scutes in the nostrils, and a layer of small ossicles under the head.
facts.quote: Bony plates are present across the entire exterior of the skull, including large osteoderms on all the sides of the skull and mandible, small scutes within the nostrils, and underneath the head in the form of an aggregation of small ossicles covering the surface between the two lower jaws.

facts.statement: The skull of Panoplosaurus was attached to the neck at an angle that suggests it held its head with the snout about 20 degrees below the horizontal.
facts.quote: The occipital, where the skull articulates with the neck, is short and thick, facing nearly directly downwards, which would have meant the head was held with the snout down in life, about 20 degrees below the horizontal.

facts.statement: Unlike Edmontonia, Panoplosaurus retained a groove separating cranial osteoderms, indicating a unique narrow scute across the rear of the skull.
facts.quote: Unlike in Edmontonia, the groove separating cranial osteoderms in Panoplosaurus never disappear, which show that there is a unique narrow scute across the entire rear of the skull.

facts.statement: Due to fusion and armor covering, only the predentary bone of the 310 mm long Panoplosaurus mandible could be identified.
facts.quote: Due to fusion and the covering of osteoderms, the only individual bone of the 310 mm long mandible than can be identified is the predentary.

facts.statement: The horseshoe-shaped predentaries of Panoplosaurus formed a sharp beak that fit within the overhang of the upper jaw.
facts.quote: Predentaries, which make up the lower portion of the snout, are somewhat horseshoe-shaped, form a sharp beak that fits within the overhang of the premaxillaries in the upper jaw.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus lacked teeth in both the upper and lower snout, a derived trait among nodosaurids.
facts.quote: Both the predentaries and their premaxillary counterparts lack any teeth, a derived feature among nodosaurids where premaxillary teeth are sometimes present.

facts.statement: Eight maxillary teeth were preserved in Panoplosaurus, suggesting the total tooth count was low.
facts.quote: Eight maxillary teeth are preserved, and though it is not certain that was the full tooth count there is not room for many more in the jaw.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus teeth featured a mild crown expansion above the root and denticles with more ridges on the front edge than the rear.
facts.quote: All the teeth are similar to those of Edmontonia and Palaeoscincus, with a mild expansion of the crown above the root (cingulum), and denticles formed by prominent ridges on both the front and rear edges of the crown, though there are more on the front than rear edge of the tooth.

facts.statement: The scapula and coracoid bones were completely fused in Panoplosaurus, with only a slight thickening marking the suture.
facts.quote: The scapula and coracoid are completely fused together, with the only indication of the bone separation being a slight thickening along what would be the suture.

facts.statement: The fused scapula and coracoid of Panoplosaurus measured 410 mm and 255 mm in length respectively.
facts.quote: The scapula itself is 410 mm long, and the coracoid is 255 mm.

facts.statement: The complete fusion of the scapulocoracoid is a unique characteristic of Panoplosaurus.
facts.quote: The complete fusion of the scapulocoracoid is unique to Panoplosaurus.

facts.statement: The robust 430 mm humerus of Panoplosaurus suggests its upper arm was held in a flexed position during life.
facts.quote: The humerus is a robust, 430 mm long bone, with the shape and projection of the head suggesting the upper arm of Panoplosaurus was held in a flexed position in life.

facts.statement: All claw bones of Panoplosaurus were hoof-shaped, lacking a point and having a flat bottom.
facts.quote: All ungual bones were hoof-shaped, lacking a point and bearing a flat bottom.

facts.statement: The articulated tibia and fibula of Panoplosaurus measured 385 mm and 310 mm respectively, with the tibia being noticeably longer.
facts.quote: The right tibia and fibula were found still in articulation, with the 385 mm tibia being noticeably longer than the 310 mm fibula.

facts.statement: The tibia of Panoplosaurus was shorter than its humerus, a trait shared with ankylosaurids but contrasting with Stegosaurus and basal taxa.
facts.quote: As in ankylosaurids, the tibia of Panoplosaurus was shorter than the humerus, which contrasts with Stegosaurus and basal taxa like Scelidosaurus.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus had large, paired osteoderms with a low keel that formed bands around the neck extending from the head.
facts.quote: The first kind was large, paired elements with a low keel, which formed bands around the neck leading from the head.

facts.statement: Along the sides of the neck to the back, Panoplosaurus had smaller, suboval osteoderms with a strong keel.
facts.quote: On the sides of the neck to the back was a second kind, individual elements that were slightly smaller, suboval, and had a strong keel.

facts.statement: Small, keeled scutes with a thick base occurred on the underside of the neck base extending to the chin in Panoplosaurus.
facts.quote: Small, keeled scutes with a thick base were identified as the fourth osteoderm type, occurring on the underside of the base of the neck forwards to the chin.

facts.statement: Small, irregular, non-keeled scutes were found in Panoplosaurus, possibly from the limbs, though this was not confirmed.
facts.quote: Small irregular scutes lacking a keel were identified as a sixth form, and were suggested to have been from the limbs, though this was not definitive.

facts.statement: The scutes on the top and sides of the neck in Panoplosaurus were distinct and differed significantly from those in Edmontonia.
facts.quote: The scutes along the top and sides of the neck in Panoplosaurus are the most distinct form, differing significantly from the corresponding elements in Edmontonia.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the unique short snout of the Panoplosaurus holotype is due to age or sex differences rather than species-specific traits.
facts.quote: As other nodosaurid specimens from the same location that may be referred to Panoplosaurus lack the distinctively short snout of the holotype, it may be that its unique appearance is due to it being a different age or sex than other individuals.

facts.statement: Sternberg identified the ilium support structure of Panoplosaurus in 1921, proposing six vertebrae including four true sacrals.
facts.quote: Sternberg identified that the ilium of Panoplosaurus was supported by at least six vertebrae in 1921, which he identified as a dorsosacral, four true sacral vertebrae, and a caudosacral.

facts.statement: Carpenter questioned Sternberg's 1990 identification of four sacrals in Panoplosaurus, noting Edmontonia has only three, though he could not confirm the first sacral was a dorsosacral.
facts.quote: The identification of four sacrals was questioned by Carpenter in 1990, as Edmontonia only has three true sacrals, but he was not able to definitively identify the first sacral of Sternberg as a dorsosacral.

facts.statement: Lambe named the genus Panoplosaurus in 1919.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus was originally named simply as a genus of armoured dinosaur by Lambe in 1919

facts.statement: Sternberg classified Panoplosaurus within the family Ankylosauridae in 1921.
facts.quote: it was subsequently specified by Sternberg in 1921 that within Stegosauria it was closest to taxa like Ankylosaurus and Euoplocephalus, and so within Ankylosauridae

facts.statement: Sternberg described the genus Edmontonia in 1928 as a close relative of Panoplosaurus.
facts.quote: The description of the new genus Edmontonia in 1928 by Sternberg identified it as a very close relative of Panoplosaurus

facts.statement: Franz Nopcsa proposed a new classification for Panoplosaurus in 1929 after describing Struthiosaurus.
facts.quote: Following further description of the armoured taxon Struthiosaurus by Franz Nopcsa in 1929, a different classification war proposed

facts.statement: Loris S. Russell placed Panoplosaurus in the subfamily Edmontoniinae in 1940.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus was then placed in the new subfamily Edmontoniinae by Loris S. Russell in 1940

facts.statement: Coombs synonymized Panoplosaurus with Edmontonia, leaving it as the only Late Cretaceous nodosaurid from North America.
facts.quote: Coombs synonymized Panoplosaurus with Edmontonia, making Panoplosaurus the only Late Cretaceous nodosaurid from North America

facts.statement: Tracy Ford classified Panoplosaurus alone in the subfamily Panoplosaurinae in 2000 based on osteoderm anatomy.
facts.quote: Tracy Ford published a novel classification of Panoplosaurus in 2000, using osteoderm anatomy to divide Nodosauridae into Nodosaurinae including only Nodosaurus, Sauropeltinae including Sauropelta and Silvisaurus, Edmontoniinae including Edmontonia and a distinct Chassternbergia, and Panoplosaurinae including only Panoplosaurus

facts.statement: A 1996 analysis by Yuong-Nam Lee nested Panoplosaurus mirus next to Edmontonia.
facts.quote: The first phylogenetic analysis to include Panoplosaurus was that of Yuong-Nam Lee in 1996, where Panoplosaurus mirus, including both CMN 2759 and ROM 1215 nested next to Edmontonia

facts.statement: A 2003 analysis by Robert Hill and colleagues identified Panoplosaurus as the sister taxon to a group containing Edmontonia and Animantarx.
facts.quote: The 2003 analysis of Robert Hill and colleagues resolved a group of Edmontonia and Animantarx, with Panoplosaurus as the sister taxon

facts.statement: Madzia and colleagues named the clade uniting Panoplosaurus with taxa closer to it than Nodosaurus or Struthiosaurus as Panoplosaurini.
facts.quote: Daniel Madzia and colleagues decided to name the clade uniting all taxa closer to Panoplosaurus than Nodosaurus or Struthiosaurus, giving it the formal name Panoplosaurini

facts.statement: The variability in Panoplosaurus teeth implies a less restrictive feeding strategy than a simple soft-food diet.
facts.quote: While the shape of teeth in Panoplosaurus and other ankylosaurs suggests a simple, soft food diet, their variability implies a less restrictive feeding strategy

facts.statement: Microwear on Panoplosaurus teeth indicates a diet of abundant foliage with occasional fruit.
facts.quote: microwear on the teeth of ankylosaurids and Panoplosaurus instead show that their diets were not significantly different, with regular pitting and abrasion showing a diet consisting occasionally of fruit as well as more abundant foliage

facts.statement: It is uncertain whether Panoplosaurus possessed gastroliths, as they were not identified in the original specimen material.
facts.quote: Gastroliths may have been found with Panoplosaurus as well, but their identification is uncertain as they were not originally mentioned among the material found as part of the specimen

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses have consistently placed Panoplosaurus in a group with Edmontonia, but its exact position relative to other nodosaurids like Animantarx and Texasetes remains debated.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus was continually found within a group including Edmontonia and also at times Animantarx, Texasetes, Denversaurus (if considered separate from Edmontonia) and Patagopelta

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus had a nasal passage that performed two full 360-degree loops in different planes before reaching the olfactory recess.
facts.quote: The complete nasal passage of Panoplosaurus undergoes two complete 360 degree loops in different planes along its length, before entering the olfactory recess for scent processing.

facts.statement: Simulations suggest air passing through Panoplosaurus's nasal passages warmed by 17.9 to 18.2 degrees Celsius and became saturated with moisture.
facts.quote: Inflowing air in Panoplosaurus was simulated to undergo a raise of between 17.9 and 18.2 C, primarily in the elongate nasal passage, while saturating the air with moisture.

facts.statement: The brain of Panoplosaurus occupied 33% of the skull's length, a proportion higher than in other ankylosaurids.
facts.quote: The brain of Panoplosaurus takes up 33% of the length of the skull, similar to the nodosaurid Pawpawsaurus where the value is 30%, a higher value than in ankylosaurids.

facts.statement: River channels in Panoplosaurus's habitat could exceed 200 meters in width and flowed east toward the Bearpaw Sea.
facts.quote: Some channel widths may even have exceeded 200 m, flowing east towards the Bearpaw Sea across the coastal plain.

facts.statement: The ground in Panoplosaurus's environment was covered with mosses, lichens, fungi, and decaying plant matter.
facts.quote: The ground would have been covered with mosses, lichens, and fungi, and a layer of decaying plant matter.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus lived in a landscape resembling the swampy coastal plains of modern-day Carolina.
facts.quote: The landscape would have resembled the swampy coastal plains of the modern Carolinas.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was a compact dinosaur measuring 5 to 7 meters in length, 2 meters in height, and weighing approximately 1.5 to 1.6 tonnes.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus fue un dinosaurio de constitución compacta de entre 5 a 7 metros de largo y 2 de alto, llegando a pesar cerca de 1,5 a 1,6 toneladas de peso.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was heavily armored with transverse bands of studded plates covering its back and tail, but likely lacked the club found in ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: Estaba fuertemente blindado, incluso para los estándares de otros nodosáuridos, probablemente con bandas transversales de placas tachonadas que cubrían su espalda y cola, aunque la cola probablemente carecía del garrote que se encuentra en los anquilosaurios.

facts.statement: Its heavy armor consisted of sharp spikes along the sides of the neck, shoulders, and sides of the thorax and belly.
facts.quote: Su pesada armadura estaba compuesta por espinas afiladas a los lados del cuello, hombros y costados del tórax y vientre.

facts.statement: It had a narrow head with eye spikes and a blade-like mouth for stripping plants, connected to the body by a short neck protected by square plates.
facts.quote: La cabeza era angosta con púas sobre los ojos y con una boca con dientes como laminas para desgajar las plantas, que se unía al cuerpo por un corto cuello protegido por placas cuadradas.

facts.statement: The head armor fused into a compact helmet-like shield with bulging surfaces, and bony shields were present on the cheeks.
facts.quote: La armadura de la cabeza se fundió en un escudo compacto parecido a un casco, estas placas tenían una superficie abultada. También estaban presentes escudos huesudos en las mejillas.

facts.statement: Unlike some other nodosaurs, Panoplosaurus lacked shoulder spikes.
facts.quote: Los picos en el hombro, que presentaban algunos otros nodosáuridos, estaban ausentes.

facts.statement: It had a relatively narrow snout, possibly to help pull low plant shoots.
facts.quote: Este animal tenía un hocico relativamente estrecho, quizás para ayudar a arrancar los brotes de las plantas bajas comían.

facts.statement: Its front legs were particularly strong with large muscle insertions, suggesting it might have been surprisingly agile and capable of defensive charges like a modern rhinoceros.
facts.quote: Las patas delanteras eran particularmente fuertes, y tenían grandes inserciones para músculos grandes, que pueden sugerir que el animal habría sido asombrosamente ágil en vida, posiblemente pudiendo hacer cargas de la defensiva como un moderno rinoceronte.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 79 to 73 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 79 y 73 millones de años, en el Campaniense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The first fossil was found in 1917 by Charles M. Sternberg at Quarry 8 near Little Sandhill Creek.
facts.quote: El primer fósil fue encontrado en 1917 por Charles M. Sternberg en Quarry 8, cerca de Little Sandhill Creek.

facts.statement: The type species Panoplosaurus mirus was named by Lawrence M. Lambe in 1919.
facts.quote: La especie tipo Panoplosaurus mirus fue nombrada por Lawrence M. Lambe en 1919.

facts.statement: The generic name derives from the Greek words pan, meaning "completely," and hoplon, meaning "armor."
facts.quote: El nombre genérico se deriva del griego pan, "completamente" y hoplon, "armadura".

facts.statement: The holotype, CMN 2759, was discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation dating to the late middle Campanian, approximately 76 million years ago.
facts.quote: Este holotipo , CMN 2759, fue descubierto en la Formación Dinosaur Park que data del Campaniano medio tardío, hace 76 millones de años.

facts.statement: Two larger specimens, ROM 1215 and RTMP 83.25.2, were later found, providing information on the shoulder girdle and forelimbs in addition to skulls.
facts.quote: Posteriormente se encontraron dos especímenes más grandes, que nuevamente contenían cráneos pero que también brindaban información sobre la cintura escapular y las extremidades anteriores, ROM 1215 y RTMP 83.25.2.

facts.statement: Specimens of Panoplosaurus have also been reported from the Aguja Formation.
facts.quote: También se han reportado especímenes de Panoplosaurus de la Formación Aguja.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus belonged to the family Nodosauridae within the suborder Ankylosauria of the Thyreophora.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus perteneció a la familia Nodosauridae dentro del infraorden Ankylosauria de los Thyreophora.

facts.statement: Originally assigned to Ankylosauridae, Panoplosaurus is now considered a member of Nodosauridae as a close relative of Edmontonia from the same formation.
facts.quote: Originalmente asignado a Ankylosauridae, Panoplosaurus se considera hoy un miembro de Nodosauridae como un pariente cercano de Edmontonia de la misma formación.

facts.statement: The genus Panoplosaurus existed from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus mirus is the only known species in the extinct genus Panoplosaurus.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus mirus es la única especie conocida del género extinto Panoplosaurus

facts.statement: In 1971, Walter Coombs referred the species Edmontonia to a subgenus within Panoplosaurus, creating Panoplosaurus (Edmontonia) longiceps and Panoplosaurus (Edmontonia) rugosidens, but this has not found lasting acceptance.
facts.quote: En 1971, Walter Coombs incluso refirió la especie de Edmontonia a un subgénero dentro de Panoplosaurus, creando un Panoplosaurus (Edmontonia) longiceps y un Panoplosaurus (Edmontonia) rugosidens, pero esto no ha encontrado una aceptación duradera.
